clue.text: Raincoat might be this one thrown out by waiter — horrible!

indicators.note: the one is ejected from the word waiter, as a bouncer throws someone out of a place

parts.note: taken as written before the one is removed
the Roman numeral for one
something horrible is repellent, disgusting

explanation.surface: A waiter is so dreadful that one customer gets kicked out of the restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: The em dash makes 'horrible' look like a verdict on the waiter, but it is simply the second half of the charade.
explanation.definitionFit: A raincoat is designed to keep moisture off, so its fabric is described as shedding rain rather than soaking it up.

clue.text: Meander with graduate, golf bore

parts.note: to meander is to wind, twisting along
a BA is a Bachelor of Arts
G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Wandering around the course with a graduate, golf proves tedious.
explanation.definitionFit: A windbag is a person who talks at tedious length, someone who wearies others.

clue.text: Superior pedestrian crossing?

definitions.meaning: sounds like a walker of high quality, but means one who walks high up
suggests a zebra crossing on a road, but means crossing on a high wire

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pedestrian crossing' is a road feature; read apart, it is someone walking far above the crowd along a taut line.
explanation.definitionFit: A tightrope walker is an acrobat who crosses on a taut high wire, literally a walker above.

clue.text: Curses rodents

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an exclamation of annoyance
second meaning: animals of the genus Rattus

explanation.walkthrough: One short word serves both as a cry of irritation and as the plural of a common rodent.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an expletive of vexation and the plural name of long-tailed vermin.

clue.text: Somewhat fidgety Monday, the very beginning of term?

indicators.note: only part of the phrase fidgety Monday is used, its letters lying across the two words

parts.note: the letters run on from the end of fidgety into the start of Monday

explanation.surface: A child restless on the first Monday of the school term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Term' suggests a school term; it means a word, whose very beginning is its root form.
explanation.definitionFit: An etymon is the original root word from which a later word derives, so it is the origin of a vocabulary item.

clue.text: Effort in manoeuvring entire ox

indicators.note: the letters are steered into a new arrangement, as one might manoeuvre a large animal

parts.note: rearranged
rearranged

explanation.surface: It takes real effort to steer a whole ox around.
explanation.definitionFit: Exertion is physical or mental effort, the strenuous use of strength.

clue.text: US city is deprived of housing backer

indicators.note: the backer is lodged inside the word for being deprived

parts.note: someone who is deprived of something loses it
an angel is a financial backer, especially of a theatre production

explanation.surface: An American city's people lose their homes because an investor pulled out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housing' reads as homes for people, but it is the instruction to put one word inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: Los Angeles is the large Californian city on the Pacific coast, home of Hollywood.

clue.text: New in Commons, stepson ignoring leader is insane

indicators.note: the letters are made new, put into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the first letter of stepson is disregarded

parts.note: loses its opening letter

explanation.surface: A new MP in the House of Commons whose stepson is ignoring the party leader is mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New in Commons' reads as a freshly elected member, but New is the anagram signal and 'in Commons' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Non compos mentis is Latin for 'not in control of one's mind', a legal phrase for being of unsound mind.

clue.text: Legendary magician gets the bird

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the wizard of Arthurian legend

explanation.surface: A legendary wizard gets the bird, as if being booed off stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets the bird' is an idiom for being jeered, but here it only joins the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Merlin was King Arthur's wizard, and a merlin is also a small falcon of moors and heathland.

clue.text: No king chivalrous every twenty-four hours

indicators.note: 'No king' says the word for chivalrous is to be left without its king

parts.note: chivalry is the code of knights, so chivalrous behaviour is knightly
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A lament that no monarch today behaves gallantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done each night recurs once in every full day, so it happens on a daily cycle.

clue.text: Spirit of German city noticeable in the centre

parts.note: Essen is a city in the Ruhr region of Germany

indicators.note: only the letters at the very middle of the word noticeable are used

parts.note: its middle pair of letters is taken

explanation.surface: A town in Germany whose character is most evident in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: An essence is a concentrated extract, and spirit likewise means the distilled core or vital quality of something.

clue.text: Cricketer, Hampshire's opener, taps run here

parts.note: a batsman in cricket is often called a bat

indicators.note: the opening letter of the county name is used, and an opener is also a cricket term

parts.note: its first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A Hampshire cricketer opening the batting, with a stray run thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: Hampshire is an English county with a cricket team, and opener is the batsman who goes in first, so the cricket picture hides a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A bathtub is the fixture into which water runs from its taps, a playful descriptive definition.

clue.text: Padding in yarn by EastEnders character

indicators.note: the yarn is placed beside, after, the soap character's surname

parts.note: Dot Cotton was a long-running character in the BBC soap EastEnders
wool is spun yarn

explanation.surface: Stuffing made from knitting yarn by a soap opera character.
explanation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a British TV soap set in London's East End; Dot Cotton was among its best-known characters.
explanation.definitionFit: Fluffy raw cotton fibres are used as soft wadding to cushion and protect, so it serves as padding.

clue.text: Awfully harsh snob bored by wife's potato cakes

indicators.note: the wife's letter drills into the middle of the jumbled letters
the words harsh and snob are badly jumbled

parts.note: rearranged
rearranged
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A dreadfully rude snob is made to feel tedious by his wife's fried potato.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bored' reads as weary, but it means drilled into.
explanation.definitionFit: Hash browns are patties of grated fried potato, eaten especially at breakfast.

clue.text: Harry Secombe possibly tense around American

parts.note: Harry Secombe was one of the Goons, the radio comedy team, so he is an example of a goon

indicators.note: around here means the other way round, so the American letter comes before the tense letter

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: Harry Secombe, perhaps, being stiff and anxious around an American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry Secombe' looks like one name, but 'Harry' is the verb definition. Secombe was in The Goon Show, a 1950s BBC radio comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry someone is to nag or pester them persistently, which is what go on at means.

clue.text: Simple witticism after Sherlock broadcast?

indicators.note: the witticism follows the detective's name
on air the detective's surname is heard rather than seen, so its sound is used

parts.note: Sherlock Holmes, the fictional detective
a pun is a play on words

explanation.surface: A plain little joke following a Sherlock Holmes radio programme.
explanation.walkthrough: Holmes, said aloud, loses its L and sounds like homes.
explanation.definitionFit: Homespun originally meant cloth spun at home, hence plain, unsophisticated and simple.

clue.text: Manager backing me, before ruse starts to exasperate ref

indicators.note: the reversed word comes ahead of the ruse
in this down clue the word me is reversed, backing up

parts.note: taken as written before reversal
a ploy is a cunning tactic

indicators.note: only the first letter of each following word is used

parts.note: first letters taken

explanation.surface: A football manager supports me before using a trick to annoy the referee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manager' reads as a football boss, but the definition just means someone who hires staff.
explanation.definitionFit: An employer is the person or company running a business who hires and directs workers.

clue.text: Poetic device daughter associated with laughter?

definitions.meaning: the definition: a technique used in verse
the example: these two words look as if they rhyme on the page but are pronounced differently

explanation.walkthrough: Daughter and laughter share their spelling ending but not their sound, the textbook case of a rhyme that works only for the reader's eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A pairing of words whose spellings match while their pronunciations differ is a recognised device in poetry.

clue.text: Man forgetting article to be distributed in Bury

indicators.note: the letters are scattered into a new order
the article is left out of the word man

parts.note: taken as written before the article goes
a is the indefinite article
taken as written

explanation.surface: An absent-minded man forgets a parcel that should be delivered to Bury.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is a town in Greater Manchester, which makes it look like a delivery address; here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To entomb is to place a body in a tomb, a synonym for laying the dead to rest.

clue.text: Perhaps Chester was spinning something in the playground

parts.note: Chester is the seat of a bishop, a see, so it is an example of one

indicators.note: the word was spins round to read the other way

parts.note: taken as written before it is turned

explanation.surface: Someone called Chester was twirling around on the playground equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: Chester reads as a child's name, but it is the English cathedral city whose diocese is a see.
explanation.definitionFit: A seesaw is a plank balanced on a pivot that children ride up and down at play areas.

clue.text: Dog holding up wife of footballer, maybe winger

indicators.note: in a down answer the second piece sits below and supports the first

parts.note: WAG, from 'wives and girlfriends', is British tabloid slang for footballers' partners
to dog someone is to tail or follow them

explanation.surface: A dog delays a footballer's wife, perhaps one married to a winger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winger' reads as a wide footballer, but it means a bird, something with wings.
explanation.definitionFit: A wagtail is a small songbird known for bobbing its tail, so it is a flying creature.

clue.text: Fancy a dip?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: as a verb, to like or enjoy
second meaning: a sauce or chutney to eat with food

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy a dip?' reads as an invitation to swim, but it is two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To relish something is to enjoy it, and a relish is a tangy condiment served with food.

clue.text: Might it carry milk dispenser, bread and last bits of lime jelly?

definitions.text: Might it carry milk dispenser, bread and last bits of lime jelly?

parts.note: a teat is what an animal's milk comes from
a roll is a small loaf of bread

indicators.note: only the final letter of each of these words is used

parts.note: the last letter of each word is taken

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a trolley might bear milk, bread and lime jelly for tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and a picture of what such a trolley carries: a milk jug, bread and jelly.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea trolley is a wheeled serving cart for bringing round cups, milk and snacks at teatime.

clue.text: Composer a little flabbergasted

indicators.note: just a small part of the word flabbergasted is used

parts.note: the composer's name sits in the middle of this long word

explanation.surface: A composer who is somewhat astonished.
explanation.definitionFit: Alban Berg was an Austrian composer of the Second Viennese School, a pupil of Schoenberg.

clue.text: Greek cheese in hamper, it's said

indicators.note: the word for hamper is used as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: to fetter is to restrict, to hamper

explanation.surface: A Greek cheese packed in a picnic basket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamper' looks like a picnic basket, but it is the verb meaning to restrain.
explanation.definitionFit: Feta is a white brined cheese from Greece, made from sheep's or goat's milk.

clue.text: Rouse ex-PM for Spooner and step aside

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so these two words have their first letters exchanged

parts.note: to rouse is to wake
Theresa May was a British Prime Minister

explanation.surface: Wake up a former Prime Minister and then get out of the way.
explanation.definitionFit: To make way is to move aside so that someone else can pass, the same idiom as stepping aside.

clue.text: Hip injured, irate disinclination to move

parts.note: in means fashionable, the same as hip

indicators.note: the word irate is hurt into a new arrangement

parts.note: rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone with a damaged hip is angry and reluctant to get moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hip injured' reads as the body part, but hip is the slang word for trendy.
explanation.definitionFit: Inertia is the tendency of a body or person to stay at rest and resist being set in motion.

clue.text: Show trial with no one in the gallery?

definitions.meaning: reads as a political sham trial, but means a trial run of a show

definitions.text: with no one in the gallery
definitions.meaning: suggests an empty court's public gallery, but means a theatre with no audience yet

explanation.walkthrough: A show trial is a staged court case; here it is a practice run of a stage show, played before the audience is admitted.
explanation.definitionFit: The final full run-through of a play in costume, before an audience is present, is its last practice.
